units.t: Evolution & Genetics. Episode one.
In this episode: How evolution works, DNA: your body's instruction manual and Genes and inheritance.
Part one. How evolution works.
No designer, no plan, just time, variation and small differences adding up over millions of years.
Darwin and variation.
In 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, arguing that living things change over generations through natural selection.
His voyage on HMS Beagle stopped in Sydney and Hobart in 1836.
Alfred Russel Wallace, working in South-East Asia, reached the same idea independently, and their work was presented together in 1858.
It became the foundation of modern biology.
The raw material is variation.
No two individuals are exactly alike: some giraffes have longer necks, some moths are darker, some bacteria resist a drug.
Much of it comes from genes passed to offspring.
New variation arises from mutations, small random changes in DNA, and from the reshuffling of genes in sexual reproduction.
Most mutations are neutral or harmful, but occasionally one helps.
Selection, not strength.
Every species produces more offspring than can survive.
A cod can release millions of eggs, and even slow-breeding elephants would overrun the planet if every calf lived.
So individuals compete for food, mates and safety.
Those whose traits suit their environment are slightly more likely to survive and have young.
Over many generations, helpful traits become more common.
That's natural selection: simple, relentless and unguided.
'Survival of the fittest', a phrase coined by philosopher Herbert Spencer, is often misunderstood.
It doesn't mean the strongest survive.
'Fittest' means best suited to a particular environment: perhaps the best camouflaged, the most cooperative or the one needing the least food.
A trait that helps in one place can hurt in another, and evolution has no goal.
It keeps whatever works well enough, right now.
Evolution in action.
Peppered moths in England were mostly pale, speckled like lichen on tree bark.
During the Industrial Revolution, soot killed the lichen and blackened the trees.
Within decades, dark moths became far more common around industrial cities, because birds spotted and ate pale moths more easily.
When clean-air laws cut pollution in the late 20th century, pale moths bounced back.
Bacteria evolve even faster, sometimes reproducing every 20 minutes.
When antibiotics kill most bacteria in an infection, any with a lucky mutation survive and multiply, and repeating this produces resistant 'superbugs'.
That's why doctors say to take antibiotics exactly as prescribed and not for viral infections like colds.
Insects evolving resistance to pesticides works the same way.
The evidence.
Evolution is supported by several independent lines of evidence.
Fossils show changing life forms through time, including transitional species like early whales with legs.
DNA comparisons show how closely species are related; humans and chimpanzees share roughly 98 to 99 per cent of their aligned DNA sequence.
Anatomy reveals shared designs, like the same bones in a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper.
And we observe evolution directly in bacteria, insects and even Darwin's finches in the Galapagos.
Deep time and us.
Earth is about 4.
5 billion years old, and life appeared at least 3.
5 billion years ago.
That's enough time for small changes to add up to the enormous variety of life today.
Humans didn't evolve from modern chimpanzees; we share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 7 million years ago.
Our own species, Homo sapiens, appeared in Africa around 300,000 years ago.
Go back far enough and every living thing, from koalas to mushrooms, shares a common ancestor.
The key idea: Natural selection acts on genetic variation between individuals, which comes from mutations and reshuffled genes.
Part two. DNA: your body's instruction manual.
Two metres of code in every cell, written in a four-letter alphabet.
The code of life.
DNA, short for deoxyribonucleic acid, carries the instructions for building and running almost every living thing, from bacteria to blue whales.
It's found inside nearly every cell in your body.
Unwound and laid end to end, the DNA in a single human cell would stretch about two metres, yet it's packed into a nucleus too small to see without a microscope.
In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick published its structure: a double helix, like a twisted ladder.
Their model relied heavily on X-ray images by Rosalind Franklin, especially 'Photo 51', and on data from Maurice Wilkins.
Watson, Crick and Wilkins won the 1962 Nobel Prize.
Franklin had died of cancer in 1958, aged 37, and her crucial role is now widely recognised.
A four-letter alphabet.

The rungs of the DNA ladder are made of four chemical bases: adenine, A, thymine, T, cytosine, C, and guanine, G. A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. That means each strand is a complementary template for the other, so a cell can copy its DNA by unzipping the ladder and building new partner strands.
The human genome contains about 3 billion of these base pairs.
From gene to protein.
To use a gene, a cell first copies it into messenger RNA, which carries the instructions out of the nucleus to protein-building machines called ribosomes.
Ribosomes read the message three letters at a time.
Each three-letter 'word', called a codon, calls for one of 20 amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, or signals where to stop.
Four letters give 64 possible codons, so most amino acids have several, which means some spelling changes make no difference to the protein.
In 1961, Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei decoded the first codon, starting a race that cracked the whole code by the mid-1960s.
Mutations and variation.
Every time a cell divides, it copies its 3 billion letters and occasionally makes a mistake.
Radiation, like UV from the sun, and chemicals, like those in tobacco smoke, can also damage DNA.
These changes are mutations.
Most are harmless or quickly repaired.
Some cause disease, including many cancers, which is one reason sun protection matters in Australia.
Occasionally a mutation is useful, and over generations such changes are the raw material for evolution.
Any two people share about 99.
9 per cent of their DNA.
The remaining 0.
1 per cent, around 3 million letters, accounts for differences in appearance and some disease risks.
There's more genetic variation within any so-called racial group than between groups, so scientists consider race a social idea rather than a clear biological category.
Reading and matching DNA.
The Human Genome Project, an international effort to read an entire human genome, finished in 2003 after 13 years at a cost of about US$2.
7 billion.
Today a genome can be sequenced in about a day for a few hundred dollars.
Doctors can diagnose rare genetic diseases in babies, match cancer treatments to a tumour's mutations and track viruses in real time, as in the COVID-19 pandemic.
In 1984, Alec Jeffreys found that repeated stretches of DNA vary so much between people they form a pattern almost unique to each person, identical twins aside.
DNA fingerprinting settled a 1985 immigration case, cleared an innocent man who had confessed and, in 1988, helped convict the real killer.
Modern profiles compare short repeated sequences at around 20 places in the genome.
The key idea: DNA carries the instructions for building and running living things, and its double-helix structure was revealed in 1953.
Part three. Genes and inheritance.
Why do you have your mother's eyes but your grandfather's chin, and why can two siblings look like strangers?
Genes are recipes.
A gene is a section of DNA that holds instructions, usually for building a particular protein.
Proteins do most of the work in your body, from carrying oxygen to colouring your eyes.
Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes, packed into 23 pairs of chromosomes inside almost every cell.
One chromosome in each pair came from your mother and one from your father, so you carry two copies of most genes.
Different versions of the same gene are called alleles.
One allele might produce more pigment, another less, and the combination you inherit shapes the result.
Mendel's peas.
Gregor Mendel, a monk in what is now the Czech Republic, crossed thousands of pea plants between about 1856 and 1863, tracking traits like flower colour and plant height.
Traits didn't blend: tall crossed with short gave tall, not medium.
Some versions mask others.
A dominant allele shows with one copy; a recessive allele needs two, one from each parent.
Purple crossed with white peas gave all purple.
But when those plants bred together, white flowers returned in about one in four offspring, roughly three to one.
The white allele was hidden, not lost.
Mendel published in 1866 and was largely ignored; around 1900 three scientists independently rediscovered his work.
Hidden carriers.
Because recessive alleles can hide, many people carry one copy of a gene variant linked to a genetic condition without any sign of it.
Cystic fibrosis is a well-known example: roughly 1 in 25 Australians carries a cystic fibrosis variant.
If two carriers have a child, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of the child inheriting two copies, a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier, and a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting neither.
This is why reproductive carrier screening is offered in Australia; a GP or genetic counsellor can explain the options.
Why traits and siblings vary.
Mendel chose traits controlled mainly by one gene.
Most human traits are messier.
Height involves thousands of genetic variants, each with a tiny effect, plus childhood nutrition and health.
Eye colour involves several genes, which is why two blue-eyed parents can occasionally have a brown-eyed child.
Environment matters too: genes load the dice, but diet, experience and chance help decide the roll.
Siblings differ because each egg or sperm carries one chromosome from each of 23 pairs, chosen at random, allowing over 8 million combinations.
Crossing over, where chromosomes swap segments, shuffles genes further.
Full siblings share about half of the DNA that varies between people, on average.
Identical twins share almost all of it.
X-linked traits.
Genes on the X chromosome behave unusually.
Most females have two X chromosomes; most males have one X and a much smaller Y. If a male inherits a recessive variant on his single X, no second copy masks it.
That is why red-green colour blindness affects roughly 1 in 12 men of northern European ancestry but only about 1 in 200 women.
Haemophilia follows the same pattern, usually passing from carrier mothers to sons.
If a condition appears in several relatives, mention it to your GP, who may suggest screening or a genetic counsellor.
A gene variant linked to disease often raises risk rather than guaranteeing illness, and lifestyle matters for conditions like heart disease.
Consumer DNA tests vary in accuracy for health claims.
The key idea: A gene is a stretch of DNA carrying instructions for a protein, and you inherit two copies of most genes.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Where does the variation that natural selection works on come from?
Answer. Genetic differences from mutations and gene reshuffling.
Question two. What does DNA do in a living cell?
Answer. It stores instructions for building an organism.
Question three. What does a gene usually contain?
Answer. Instructions for building a protein.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
